p067.lead: The betrayal of the Planetary Prince Caligastia and the seven years of testing: how the rebellion unfolded, and the story of Van and Amadon, who never wavered.

p067.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p067.s0.h: Introduction — Why We Need to Know About the Rebellion
p067.s0.b0: Paper 67 deals with the darkest turning point in Urantia’s history, the planetary rebellion. Its author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, says that the problems of human existence on this world cannot be understood without knowing of it. The rebellion did not seriously disturb biologic evolution, but it markedly changed the direction of social evolution and spiritual development.

p067.s0.b1.q: Although this upheaval did not seriously interfere with the progress of organic evolution, it did markedly modify the course of social evolution and of spiritual development.

p067.s0.b2: The paper is a historical record and, at the same time, a short philosophy of sin. It sets side by side a leader who betrayed his trust and fell, and an ordinary human being who stood firm under the same pressure. And it calmly distinguishes how far the consequences of sin reach and where they stop.
p067.s1.h: I. The Caligastia Betrayal — The Sin of a Broken Trust
p067.s1.b0: Caligastia had been in charge of Urantia for three hundred thousand years when Satan, Lucifer’s assistant, made one of his periodic inspection calls. Satan looked nothing like the familiar caricatures; he was a Lanonandek Son of great brilliance. He told Caligastia of Lucifer’s proposed “⟦Q 67:1.2⟧Declaration of Liberty,⟦/Q⟧” and the Prince agreed to betray the planet when the rebellion was announced.
p067.s1.b1: The author treats this betrayal with special gravity. No trust is more sacred than that of a Planetary Prince responsible for the welfare of evolving mortals, and no evil is more destructive of personality than betraying those who rely on us. By this deliberate sin Caligastia so distorted his personality that his mind has never fully regained its equilibrium.

p067.s1.b2.q: of all forms of evil, none are more destructive of personality status than betrayal of trust and disloyalty to one’s confiding friends.

p067.s1.b3: The section then distinguishes error, evil, sin, and iniquity. They can be read as stages in one’s attitude toward reality, with the will more deeply involved at each step.

p067.s1.b5: Sin chosen again and again can become habitual, and habitual sinners can easily become iniquitous. All manner of sins may be forgiven, but the author doubts whether the established iniquiter would ever sincerely feel sorrow or accept forgiveness. It reads as a warning that repeated small choices finally set the direction of a personality.
p067.s2.h: II. The Outbreak of Rebellion — A Planet Cut Off
p067.s2.b0: Shortly after Satan’s inspection, in the midwinter of the northern continents, Daligastia called the ten councils into extraordinary session. Caligastia, he announced, was about to proclaim himself absolute sovereign of Urantia, and every administrative group was to resign its powers into Daligastia’s hands. Van, chairman of the supreme council of co-ordination, branded this an act bordering on planetary rebellion and urged all to abstain until an appeal could be taken to Lucifer.

p067.s2.b2.q: Meantime the system circuits had been severed; Urantia was isolated.

p067.s2.b3: Isolation was a test for celestial beings too. Seraphim, cherubim, and other groups that happened to be on the planet had to choose between sin and righteousness, between the ways of Lucifer and the will of the unseen Father. For more than seven years the authorities of Edentia did not intervene, until every personality concerned had made a final decision. Here we see the universe’s way of respecting each one’s choice rather than forcing it.
p067.s3.h: III. The Seven Crucial Years — A Time When Mind and Spirit Were Tested
p067.s3.b0: When the rebellion was broadcast, the whole system of Satania was quarantined, and “⟦Q 67:3.1⟧war in heaven⟦/Q⟧” spread to every planet. On Urantia forty of the one hundred, including Van, refused to join the insurrection. But almost half of the administrator and transition seraphim, and 40,119 primary midway creatures, sided with Caligastia. The loyalists lived in a poorly protected settlement east of Dalamatia, guarded by loyal midwayers, and kept the tree of life.
p067.s3.b1: The author lists the reasons Van could not be shaken: clear thinking, wise reasoning, sincere motivation, intelligent loyalty, disciplined character, and the unquestioning dedication of his personality to doing the Father’s will. Loyalty, in other words, is not a passing feeling but the fruit of a long-cultivated inner life.

p067.s3.b2.q: This seven years of waiting was a time of heart searching and soul discipline.

p067.s3.b3: The most striking passage contrasts Caligastia with Amadon. Amadon, a descendant of Andon and Fonta and Van’s human assistant, stood unmoved by the sophistries of Daligastia for all seven years. The size of one’s intelligence and experience does not guarantee loyalty, and a consecrated will, in contact with the indwelling spirit, can find amazing strength.

p067.s3.b5.q: Mind and spirit, when fully united, are potential for the creation of superhuman values, even morontia realities.

p067.s4.h: IV–V. The Caligastia One Hundred after Rebellion; Immediate Results of Rebellion
p067.s4.b0: At the final roll call the Prince’s staff divided clearly along council lines. The forty who remained loyal were later transferred to Jerusem, where they resumed their Paradise journey. The sixty who rebelled chose Nod as their leader, but they soon lost the sustenance of the system life circuits and were degraded to the status of mortal beings.

p067.s4.b2: The descendants of the rebel staff became known as the Nodites, and their mingling with the peoples of earth gave rise to stories of gods coming down to mate with mortals. Without spiritual sustenance they eventually died a natural death, and much later idolatry grew out of the wish to honor their memory. The final fate of the sixty still awaits adjudication, and the text records the hope that all sincere penitents will be rehabilitated.
p067.s4.b3: Caligastia tried to rebuild society all at once according to his own ideas of freedom. But for those who were not ready, liberty became license; when revolution displaced evolution, confusion and regression followed. One hundred and sixty-two years after the rebellion a tidal wave swept over Dalamatia. The lesson is that hasty reform can lead to an even deeper retreat.

p067.s4.b4.q: Liberty was quickly translated into license by the half-evolved primitive men of those days.

p067.s5.b0: Van’s followers withdrew to the highlands west of India and there planned the rehabilitation of the world. Van placed human affairs in the hands of ten commissions of four each, and when the loyal staff returned to Jerusem the Amadonites took up these responsibilities. The Amadonites were the group of 144 loyal Andonites—thirty-nine men and one hundred and five women—who became the “biologic leaven” that furnished leadership through the long dark ages after the rebellion.
p067.s5.b1: Urantia was then governed by a council of twelve Melchizedek receivers, whose policies Van faithfully carried out. Within a thousand years of the rebellion he had more than three hundred and fifty advanced groups scattered over the world. Sustained by the tree of life and the special ministry of the Melchizedeks, Van and Amadon lived for over one hundred and fifty thousand years, fostering human evolution until the coming of Adam.
p067.s5.b2: The text adds a remarkable fact. The Constellation Fathers of Edentia had immediately sustained Van’s appeal on every point, but the decision never reached him because the circuits were cut; it lay lodged in a relay energy transmitter until it was recently discovered through the investigations of the midwayers. Justice may come to light late, but it is not lost.
p067.s6.h: VII. Remote Repercussions of Sin — Personal and Collective Consequences
p067.s6.b0: This section is the theological heart of the paper. The author divides the consequences of sin in two directions: the personal consequences reaped by the creature who rejects light, and the impersonal consequences shared by all who live within its range of effect. Fifty thousand years after the rebellion, mankind had gained very little over its condition when Caligastia arrived.

p067.s6.b2: From this distinction comes the paper’s most comforting conclusion. Sin greatly delayed the progress of civilization and society, but it cannot prevent the spiritual achievement of any individual who chooses to know God and do his will. No one’s eternal survival is endangered by another’s sin.

p067.s6.b3.q: never does the sin of any being rob another of the realization of the divine right of personality survival.

p067.s6.b4.q: No person is ever made to suffer vital spiritual deprivation because of the sin of another.

p067.s7.h: VIII. The Human Hero of the Rebellion — Amadon
p067.s7.b0: The author recalls the exhilaration he felt on Edentia as he read the Salvington broadcasts of those days. The records of Salvington portray Amadon as the outstanding character of the entire system. For seven years one question came first from all subordinate celestial life.

p067.s7.b1.q: “What of Amadon of Urantia, does he still stand unmoved?”

p067.s7.b2: The loyalty of Amadon and his 143 comrades, the author says, has already done more good in Nebadon and Orvonton than can ever be outweighed by all the evil and sorrow of the Lucifer rebellion. It also illuminates the wisdom of the Father’s plan to recruit the Corps of Mortal Finality largely from the common clay of ascending mortals—mortals just like Amadon.
p067.s8.b0: Paper 67 shows that high position and great intelligence do not guarantee loyalty, and that the unwavering choice of one ordinary person can move a universe. It also says plainly that the confusion of the world we inherited may come from the faults of others, but that no one can block an individual’s path to God.

p067.s8.b2: Paper 68, “The Dawn of Civilization,” turns to how human society slowly built co-operation and institutions under the pressure of fear and need. Remembering how deep the setback was in this paper helps us feel the weight of the slow advance that followed.
p068.lead: From bonds born of fear and hunger, through custom and the arts of the land, to civilization: the first steps taken by human society.

p068.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek sometime stationed on Urantia

p068.s0.h: Introduction — Civilization Is Learned, Not Inherited
p068.s0.b0: Paper 68 opens a series of papers on the origin of human institutions. Its author, a Melchizedek once stationed on Urantia, announces that he will tell the story of mankind’s long struggle from a state little better than animal existence to a civilization that is real, though imperfect.
p068.s0.b1: The starting point is clear. Civilization is a racial acquirement, not a biological inheritance. The achievements of science, philosophy, and religion are not passed on through the blood, so every generation must be taught anew and the social heritage must be consciously preserved. This one paragraph explains why education and tradition matter so much.

p068.s0.b2.q: Civilization is a racial acquirement; it is not biologically inherent;

p068.s0.b3: The co-operative social order was begun by the Dalamatia teachers, and for three hundred thousand years mankind was nurtured in the idea of group activities. The text notes that different groups benefited unequally from those teachings. In keeping with the spirit of the text, this is best read as a historical observation about how much contact each people had with the teaching, not as a judgment of any people’s worth.
p068.s1.h: I. Protective Socialization — Co-operation Learned Through Fear
p068.s1.b0: Primitive man was not naturally overflowing with brotherly feeling. People learned by sad experience that “⟦Q 68:1.1⟧in union there is strength⟦/Q⟧.” Going about alone, without a mark of group membership, was fatal, so association early became the price of survival. The author notes that this lack of natural brotherly attraction still stands in the way of the brotherhood of man today.

p068.s1.b1.q: Civilization has become man’s insurance against violent death, while the premiums are paid by submission to society’s numerous law demands.

p068.s1.b2: Society was born not of a mere gathering of numbers but of the organization of intelligent co-operators. Man learns to co-operate first through fear, and later because he discovers that it is most beneficial. That is why peoples who organized early survived better, and why civilization has kept advancing despite many blunders.
p068.s1.b3: The author points to primitive social conditions that survived into his own day to show that modern cultural society is a fairly recent development. The point is not to belittle any group but to show that man’s natural individualism cannot compete with the power of organization and association. The passage invites us to imagine what the world might be like without the teaching of the Planetary Prince’s staff and the Adamic uplifters.
p068.s1.b4: The section also warns against the romance of “⟦Q 68:1.7⟧back to nature⟦/Q⟧.” The author calls it a delusion, a belief in a fictitious “golden age,” and says the only historical basis for that legend is Dalamatia and Eden. Rather than idealize the past, we are urged to look at what is still to be built.
p068.s2.h: II. Factors in Social Progression — Four Forces That Drew People Together
p068.s2.b0: The herd instinct alone cannot explain today’s social organization; much of man’s sociability is acquired. The author names four forces that first drew people together and held them there.

Its nature
What it left to society
rows: Hunger

Food saving, the first self-denial; association to meet many kinds of need
Sex love

Fear (especially ghost fear)

p068.s2.b2: The home was the first place where these forces met. The presence of a helpless baby divided the work of men and women, and from earliest times, where woman was has been regarded as the home. The text does not hide the hard lot of women in primitive times. Yet it stresses that the family was the first successful peace group, where man and woman learned to adjust their antagonisms and taught the pursuits of peace to their children.
p068.s2.b3: Marriage is explained in the same light. In evolution its purpose is the insurance of race survival rather than personal happiness, and self-gratification is incidental. Yet the arts of civilization keep increasing the pleasures of marriage and the satisfactions of family life. An institution that began for survival grows over time into a place of joy.

p068.s2.b4.q: Almost everything of lasting value in civilization has its roots in the family.

p068.s2.b5: The key warning of this section is the distinction between self-maintenance and self-gratification. Society advanced as it lessened risk and pain, but when its goal tilts toward self-gratification it moves toward extinction. The author addresses this warning directly to his own age: the twentieth-century Western civilization groaning under an overload of luxury, in which pleasure-want has superseded hunger-want.

p068.s2.b6.q: Self-maintenance builds society; unbridled self-gratification unfailingly destroys civilization.

p068.s3.h: III. Socializing Influence of Ghost Fear — Superstition That Prepared for Awe
p068.s3.b0: The author names the ghost dream as probably the greatest single factor in the evolution of human society. Animals do not imagine survival after death. Fear of the spirits of the dead was a new terror reaching beyond the basic needs of the individual, and it drove loose bands into more disciplined and better controlled groups.
p068.s3.b1: Strikingly, even this superstition is said to have served a purpose. Baseless fear prepared the mind for the later discovery that “⟦Q 68:3.3⟧the fear of the Lord⟦/Q⟧” is the beginning of wisdom, and it was designed to be replaced by the awe that revelation inspires. Even in its clumsy way, evolution was reaching toward spirituality.

p068.s3.b2.q: The baseless fears of evolution are designed to be supplanted by the awe for Deity inspired by revelation.

p068.s3.b3: But these emotions alone cannot bear the strain of society. Hunger, love, vanity, and fear draw people together, yet they also plunge them into war and bloodshed. The section concludes that the peace tendency of the human race is not a natural endowment; it comes from revealed religion, from accumulated experience, and above all from the teachings of Jesus, the Prince of Peace.
p068.s4.h: IV. Evolution of the Mores — Custom as the Thread of Continuity
p068.s4.b0: All modern social institutions grew out of primitive customs. What habit is to the individual, custom is to the group, and customs become folkways and traditions—the mores. The mores were man’s first social institution, and like language their origin was unconscious and is shrouded in mystery. Ghost fear held the mores firmly in place through the belief that the dead were jealous of the ways by which they had lived.
p068.s4.b1: Primitive man was a slave to usage, compelled to do everything from morning to night in the tribe’s way. Yet the author does not treat custom as simply evil. Its inertia was a biologic safety brake against a civilization advancing too fast, and it was the thread that held civilization together.

p068.s4.b3.q: Custom has been the thread of continuity which has held civilization together.

p068.s4.b4: A society’s survival depends on the progressive evolution of its mores. New ideas are put forward, competition follows, and time and circumstance select the fitter group. But the author firmly rejects the idea that every change has been for the better. Progress is not a straight line, and discerning retrogression is itself part of progress.
p068.s5.h: V. Land Techniques — Four Stages in the March of Civilization
p068.s5.b0: Land is the stage of society; men are the actors. The evolution of the mores always depends on the land-man ratio, and man’s land techniques plus his standards of living equal the sum total of the mores. The author divides the march of civilization, which began along the rivers of the Eastern Hemisphere, into four stages.

p068.s5.b2: Gains and losses are recorded at each stage. Herding gave leisure but broke down the earlier co-operation of the sexes and lowered woman’s dignity. Agriculture settled people at home and fostered a more peace-loving temperament. The text also notes that Adam and Eve were gardeners, not shepherds.

p068.s5.b3.q: The growing of plants exerts an ennobling influence on all races of mankind.

p068.s5.b4: On the age in which industry and cities supplement agriculture, the author speaks plainly: even the highest social developments must rest on a sound agricultural basis, and an industrial era that forgets this cannot hope to survive.
p068.s6.h: VI. Evolution of Culture — The Land-Man Ratio
p068.s6.b0: Man is a creature of the soil, and his basic struggle has always been for land. Society is governed by a law: population varies directly with the land arts and inversely with the standard of living. When land was plentiful, human life was valued; when land was scarce, life was cheapened. A shrinking yield brings the worst traits of human nature to the surface, and a growing yield fosters the better side.
p068.s6.b1: Standards of living have determined the quality rather than the mere quantity of a population. The higher the standard, the smaller the family, and standards that become too complicated or luxurious soon become suicidal. Cities multiply the power of their inhabitants for good or for evil, and the fine arts, science, and spiritual culture have thrived best in large centers supported by a suitable agricultural and industrial population.
p068.s6.b2: The text records frankly the harsh practices, such as infanticide and exposure, by which primitive tribes limited their numbers. Then it adds that very few children were killed once they had been suckled. Even in a dark and brutal age, a mother’s love proved stronger than custom.

p068.s6.b3.q: very few children were ever destroyed after having once been suckled—maternal affection is too strong.

p068.s6.b4: Finally the author foresees that if war lessens and science controls disease, population may become a great test of the wisdom of world leadership. Each change in the conditions of civilization brings new responsibilities with it.
p068.s7.b0: Paper 68 shows that civilization was not simply handed to us. People banded together out of fear, lived bound by custom, and wrestled with the land to win a little leisure. Along the way the home became the first school of peace, and even ghost fear became a preparation for true reverence. The order we enjoy is a heritage kept by countless generations, and a task we must teach again to the next.

p068.s7.b2: Paper 69, “Primitive Human Institutions,” goes on to show how the society that began here developed concrete institutions: industry and the division of labor, trade and capital, fire and animals, slavery and private property.
p069.lead: Industry and trade, capital and fire, animals and slaves, private property: the origins of primitive man’s institutions, in both their light and their shadow.

p069.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p069.s0.b0: Paper 68 asked why society arose; Paper 69 looks at the institutions that society built. The author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, notes what sets man apart from his animal ancestors: emotionally, the ability to appreciate humor, art, and religion; socially, the fact that he is a toolmaker, a communicator, and an institution builder.
p069.s0.b1: Institutions grow naturally out of long-lasting social groups, and most of them have saved labor while adding to group security. Yet the author cautions against too much pride in them. Every institution is, in the end, the accumulated mores of the past, a legacy preserved by taboo and dignified by religion.

p069.s0.b2.q: all human institutions are merely the accumulated mores of the past as they have been conserved by taboos and dignified by religion.

p069.s1.h: I. Basic Human Institutions — Three Classes
p069.s1.b0: Every institution serves some social need, but when overdeveloped it overshadows personality, diminishes initiative, and lowers the worth of the individual. So people must govern their institutions rather than be governed by them. The author sorts institutions into three classes according to the urges from which they spring.

p069.s1.b1.q: Man should control his institutions rather than permit himself to be dominated by these creations of advancing civilization.

p069.s1.b3: The three classes are closely interwoven and work as a single social mechanism. Notably, the author remarks that civilization has never evolved distinctive institutions of self-gratification. The distinction between self-maintenance and self-gratification from the previous paper carries on here.
p069.s2.h: II–III. The Dawn of Industry; The Specialization of Labor
p069.s2.b0: Primitive industry grew slowly as insurance against the terrors of famine, and man learned from animals that store food against lean days. Poverty is man’s natural estate; wealth comes from labor, knowledge, and organization. Association led to organization, and the first result of organization was the division of labor, saving both time and materials.

p069.s2.b1.q: Wealth is not a natural gift; it results from labor, knowledge, and organization.

p069.s2.b2: What drove the naturally inactive early races to work was the double demand of the struggle for existence and rising standards of living. Labor—effort by design—distinguishes man from the beast, and the author reminds us that the Prince’s staff worked and that Adam was a gardener. After a long struggle between the devotees of magic and those who exercised foresight, magic slowly gave way to self-denial and industry.

p069.s2.b3.q: The necessity for labor is man’s paramount blessing.

p069.s2.b5: The story of the smiths is intriguing. Their skill with metals won them both fear and privilege, but they abused their privileges, became universally hated, and lost out to the medicine men, who drove them from the villages. The author calls this the first contest between science and religion—and superstition won. Driven out, the smiths kept the first inns on the outskirts of the settlements.
p069.s3.h: IV–V. The Beginnings of Trade and Capital — The Great Civilizer
p069.s3.b0: Barter followed seizure by raids. At first it was silent barter, armed traders leaving their goods at a neutral spot, and women held the first markets. These market places became the first sanctuaries, later known in some lands as “⟦Q 69:4.4⟧cities of refuge.⟦/Q⟧” Modern writing itself grew out of trade records; man’s first literature was a salt advertisement.

p069.s3.b1.q: Commerce has been the great civilizer through promoting the cross-fertilization of culture.

p069.s3.b2: Capital is labor applied as a renunciation of the present in favor of the future. Hoarding food developed self-control and also created the first problems of capital and labor. The author lists eight urges that led to the accumulation of capital, and the list reveals both the bright and the dark side of human motives.

p069.s3.b4: The author gives a balanced verdict on capital. Its abuse by unfair capitalists does not alter the fact that it is the basis of modern industrial society, and through capital and invention the present generation enjoys more freedom than any before it. But he adds clearly that this is a statement of fact, not a justification of capital’s misuse.

p069.s3.b5.q: Man’s technique varies, but his disposition remains quite unchanged.

p069.s4.h: VI–VII. Fire and Animals — What Set Man Apart from the Beasts
p069.s4.b0: Primitive society rose through four instruments: fire, animals, slaves, and property. Of these, fire building by a single bound separated man from animal forever. Fire let man stay on the ground at night, encouraged evening fellowship, and, through cooking, reduced the energy spent on digestion and left strength for culture.
p069.s4.b1: The loveliest meaning of fire lies in sharing. Because one could give live coals to a neighbor without losing one’s own, fire became man’s first means of being altruistic without loss. The early home was not a building but the family gathered about the fire. Andon, the discoverer of fire, did not worship it, but many of his descendants made it a fetish, and that superstition lasted long.

p069.s4.b2.q: The early home was not a building but the family gathered about the fire, the family hearth.

p069.s4.b3: Animals were at first man’s enemies, and domestication began by accident when hunters surrounded and penned herds. The dog was the first domesticated animal, and watchdogs first made it possible for a whole clan to sleep at night. But when domestication coincided with the Caligastia confusion, many tribes treated women much as they treated their animals, and the author records this as one of the darkest chapters of human history.
p069.s5.h: VIII. Slavery as a Factor in Civilization — A Bridge and a Malady
p069.s5.b0: This section treats an uncomfortable subject from a historical viewpoint. Early captives were eaten, tortured, or sacrificed, so the text judges enslavement to have been an advance over massacre and cannibalism. Slavery compelled the invention of regulative machinery and so gave rise to the beginnings of government; it was the bridge over which society passed from chaos to order.
p069.s5.b1: Yet the author does not glorify slavery. It was oppressive, and it soon attacks society from within as the gravest of all destructive social maladies. Machinery is making the slave obsolete, but his remark that thousands today let ambition enslave them to debt applies just as well to modern readers.

p069.s5.b3.q: While the ideal of society is universal freedom, idleness should never be tolerated.

p069.s6.h: IX. Private Property — From Common Holding to Ownership
p069.s6.b0: Primitive society was virtually communal—not as a theory, but as a practical adjustment that prevented pauperism. Yet this primitive communism put a premium on idleness, stifled industry, and destroyed ambition, and it gave way to a higher order because it ran counter to four strong human proclivities.

p069.s6.b2: Private property began with things personally touched, sleeping space, fire sites, and wells, and with agriculture it expanded to land. Property was respected because it was believed to carry part of the owner’s personality. Along with property the home changed shape, and polygamy was gradually displaced by monogamy, which the author calls the slave-free ideal of the matchless association of one man and one woman. He also notes that the teachers of revealed religion were the first to proclaim that the poor could have salvation on equal terms with the rich.

p069.s6.b3.q: The right to property is not absolute; it is purely social.

p069.s6.b4: The paper’s last counsel concerns our attitude toward change. The present social order is not sacred, but when we change it we must make certain we change for the better, and we must not go back to formulas our forefathers discarded.

p069.s6.b5.q: Go forward, not backward! Let evolution proceed! Do not take a backward step.

p069.s7.b0: Paper 69 shows that the workplaces and markets, savings and possessions, and family hearths we take for granted were all won through long trial and error. Deep shadows lay along the way: superstition, exploitation, and cruelty toward women and captives. The author records the light and the shadow together and urges us to govern our institutions rather than serve them, and to move forward without haste.

p069.s7.b2: Paper 70 traces how human government evolved on the foundation of these institutions. Keeping in mind how slavery and property were bound up with the beginnings of government in this paper will make the next one easier to follow.
p070.lead: From war to council, from kings to representative government: the history of human government, rights, justice, and law as they evolved through trial and error.

p070.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p070.s0.h: Introduction — Government Is an Unconscious Development
p070.s0.b0: Following the paper on primitive institutions, Paper 70 examines the evolution of human government. The author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, observes that no sooner had man partly solved the problem of making a living than he faced the task of regulating human contacts. Industry demanded law and order, and private property made government necessary.
p070.s0.b1: On an evolutionary world antagonisms are natural, and peace is secured only by some system of social regulation. No one designed government; it grew as practices that proved their survival value became tradition. Anarchy added to misery, and so law and order slowly emerged.

p070.s0.b2.q: Government is an unconscious development; it evolves by trial and error.

p070.s1.h: I–II. The Genesis of War; The Social Value of War — Scaffolding That Needs a Substitute
p070.s1.b0: War is the natural state and heritage of evolving man, an animalistic reaction to misunderstanding and irritation, while peace measures the progress of civilization. As social groups formed, individual irritations were submerged in group feeling, and peace within the tribe was bought at the expense of peace between tribes. Those who learned the golden rule early, like the Andonites, settled disputes by beating a tree with a stick or by a public contest of ridicule.

p070.s1.b1.q: War is the natural state and heritage of evolving man; peace is the social yardstick measuring civilization’s advancement.

p070.s1.b3: The author does not hide the atrocities of ancient times committed in the name of God, but he states clearly that such things are not instigated by Deity. War was gradually refined: captives were taken, women and noncombatants were exempted, wars were declared, and sanctuary and the right of asylum were recognized.
p070.s1.b4: In the past war had social value: it imposed discipline, enforced co-operation, and fostered courage. But like slavery, it is scaffolding that must one day be abandoned. As bloodletting gave way to better remedies, so must war, and for that to happen peaceful substitutes must be found for what war once accomplished.

p070.s1.b5.q: Do not make the mistake of glorifying war;

p070.s1.b6: Industrialism, which is to replace militarism, has its own dangers. The author lists materialism and spiritual blindness, the worship of wealth-power, luxury, indolence, biologic deterioration, and standardized industrial slavery, warning that labor ennobles but drudgery benumbs. Future leaders must be found not in war but in industry, science, and social achievement.
p070.s2.h: III–IV. Early Human Associations; Clans and Tribes — Widening the Peace Group
p070.s2.b0: Real government appears only when groups larger than the family form. Families united by blood into clans, and clans evolved into tribes, which were territorial communities. War and outside pressure forced tribal organization, but it was commerce and trade that kept peace within. The author holds that peace will be promoted far more by international trade organizations than by sentimental peace planning.

p070.s2.b1.q: The gain motive is a mighty civilizer when augmented by the desire to serve.

p070.s2.b2: From an age in which strangers were killed, mankind moved to adoption, “guest friendship,” and peace treaties sealed by blood bonds, and the circle of relationship slowly widened. The peace group grew from family to clan to tribe to nation, and the author finds it most encouraging that today it reaches beyond blood ties to embrace nations. The clans served local self-government well but delayed the growth of large nations.
p070.s3.h: V–VI. The Beginnings of Government; Monarchial Government — From Council to King
p070.s3.b0: The first real governmental body was the council of the elders, which held the potential of all three functions: executive, legislative, and judicial. But as people learned that neither peace nor war can be run by a debating society, power gathered in the war chiefs. War has always been a kingmaker.

p070.s3.b2: Man discovered that effective government comes from conferring power on a personality, not on an idea. Hereditary kingship prevented the havoc of succession struggles, but it also bred the superstition of the king’s divine origin. Yet even the most despotic tyrant was restrained by fear of assassination, by priests and aristocracy, and by people who would rise up against him.
p070.s4.h: VII–VIII. Primitive Clubs and Secret Societies; Social Classes
p070.s4.b0: After blood kinship and intermarriage, the next step was religious cults and political clubs. Appearing first as secret societies, they trained adolescent youths and taught sex control, and they also served as spies, secret police, and tax collectors. Yet they became the first schools, the first political parties, and the first charitable organizations, and finally the forerunners of churches and the first international fraternities.
p070.s4.b1: The mental and physical inequality of human beings ensures that social classes will appear. The author lists ten reasons classes form: natural, personal, chance, economic, geographic, social, vocational, religious, racial, and age. Strikingly, the only worlds without social strata are the most primitive and the most advanced, and a world settled in light and life has largely effaced these divisions.
p070.s4.b2: Flexible, shifting classes are indispensable to an evolving civilization, but when class hardens into caste, stability is bought at the cost of personal initiative and social co-operation. The author foresees that classes will be dissolved over millenniums through biologic improvement, education, and a religious quickening of the sense of brotherhood.

p070.s4.b3.q: Religion is the mighty lever that lifts civilization from chaos, but it is powerless apart from the fulcrum of sound and normal mind resting securely on sound and normal heredity.

p070.s5.h: IX–X. Human Rights; Evolution of Justice — The Rules of the Game
p070.s5.b0: Nature confers no rights on man, only life and a world in which to live it. Society’s prime gift is security. The author lists ten rights that society has come to assure, the last being the guarantee of the freedom of religious practice so that all other social activities may be exalted by spiritual motivation.

p070.s5.b1.q: But human rights are not really natural; they are entirely social.

p070.s5.b2: Rights are relative and ever-changing rules of the game. Society cannot offer equal rights to all, but it can promise to administer the varying rights of each with fairness and equity. Its duty is to give everyone a fair opportunity for self-maintenance, self-perpetuation, and some measure of self-gratification, and the author sums up the three together as human happiness.
p070.s5.b3: Justice, too, is a product of evolution. Primitive man asked not what killed someone but who, and ignored motive. Through ordeals of poison and fire, blood vengeance, and blood money, true justice began only when revenge was taken from private and kin groups and lodged with the state. Of the ordeal that survives in scripture, the author insists that no divine being ever gave such unfair instructions.

p070.s5.b4.q: it was learned that the severity of the punishment was not so valuable a deterrent to crime as was its certainty and swiftness.

p070.s6.h: XI–XII. Laws and Courts; Allocation of Civil Authority — Toward Representative Government
p070.s6.b0: Mores are laws in the making, and law is a codified record of long human experience. Law begins as negative and prohibitive, like “⟦Q 70:11.2⟧you shall not kill⟦/Q⟧,” but becomes more positive and directive as civilization advances. The first courts were regulated fistic encounters, yet the status of any civilization can be accurately judged by the thoroughness and equity of its courts and the integrity of its judges.
p070.s6.b1: In early society crime was an assault on the tribal mores, and sin the transgression of taboos sanctioned by ghosts. The failure to separate the two caused long confusion, but self-interest, social tradition, and religious sanction together made human life more safe and sacred. The author judges that superstition was the moral and social police force of the long evolutionary ages.
p070.s6.b2: The great struggle in the evolution of government has concerned the concentration of power. Universe administrators have learned by experience that evolutionary peoples are best governed by representative government with a proper balance among executive, legislative, and judicial branches. The author says that Urantia mortals are entitled to liberty, and should adopt their own constitutions and choose competent and worthy leaders.

p070.s6.b4.q: While there is a divine and ideal form of government, such cannot be revealed but must be slowly and laboriously discovered by the men and women of each planet throughout the universes of time and space.

p070.s7.b0: Paper 70 shows that the peace, rights, and courts we enjoy were not handed down from heaven ready-made but refined little by little through bloodshed and trial and error. Its conclusion—that even the ideal government is not revealed but must be discovered—returns responsibility to every citizen. Peace does not come merely by wishing for it; it comes when we provide wise substitutes for what war once did.

p070.s7.b2: Paper 71, “Development of the State,” considers where this evolving government is heading: the stages of representative government and the shape of the ideal state. The discussion of the balance of power and constitutional tribunals in this paper is its starting point.
p071.lead: How the embryonic state born of conquest grows toward representative government and the ideal state, and why no state can rise above the moral level of its citizens.

p071.foot.text: Sponsored by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p071.s0.h: Introduction — The State Is an Evolved Institution
p071.s0.b0: Paper 71 rounds off the series on human institutions by asking how the state arose and where it should be heading. Sponsored by a Melchizedek of Nebadon, it does not stop at recording the past; it looks ahead, setting out the stages of representative government and the marks of the ideal state.
p071.s0.b1: The starting point is a sober definition. The state is society’s net gain from the ravages and sufferings of war; it was neither divinely founded nor deliberately designed by anyone. Along with it arose the moral myth of the citizen’s absolute obligation to live and die for the state. The paper can be read as a call not to idolize the state but to use it rightly as a tool.

p071.s0.b2.q: But the state is not of divine genesis;

p071.s1.h: I. The Embryonic State — From Blood Ties to Territory
p071.s1.b0: The state is a territorial social regulative organization, and it is strongest and most enduring when made up of a single nation sharing a common language, mores, and institutions. The early states were small and all the result of conquest, so they were stratified from the start. The embryonic state became possible when the blood bond gave way to the territorial bond.
p071.s1.b1: The author contrasts two cases. The Iroquois federation of North America had good government but lacked certain essentials of national life and never quite functioned as a state. The text says they were too democratic, and that they would eventually have evolved a state had they not prematurely encountered a more advanced civilization. Rome, by contrast, built a successful state on the foundations listed below.

p071.s1.b3: Rome too collapsed in the end. The author points to one factor: the sudden and extensive manner in which supposedly liberal reforms were adopted. The harm lay not in the reforms themselves but in their speed, and Rome shows what happens when internal degeneration is joined to too rapid expansion. When states fail to integrate, they may slip back into prestate conditions, as in the feudalism of the European Middle Ages.
p071.s2.h: II. The Evolution of Representative Government — Ten Steps
p071.s2.b0: Democracy is an ideal, but it is a product of civilization, not of evolution. So the author urges, “⟦Q 71:2.1⟧Go slowly! select carefully!⟦/Q⟧” and names its dangers: the glorification of mediocrity, the choice of base and ignorant rulers, universal suffrage in the hands of uneducated majorities, and slavery to public opinion. The majority is not always right.
p071.s2.b1: Public opinion slows society, yet it is valuable because it preserves civilization. The answer, then, is not to ignore public opinion but to educate it. The advance of society is measured by how far public opinion can control personal behavior and state regulation without violence, and cultural growth accelerates as bullets give way to ballots.

p071.s2.b2.q: Education of public opinion is the only safe and true method of accelerating civilization;

p071.s2.b3.q: Popular elections may not always decide things rightly, but they represent the right way even to do a wrong thing.

p071.s3.h: III. The Ideals of Statehood — What It Does, Not What It Is
p071.s3.b0: The form of government matters little so long as it provides liberty, security, education, and social co-ordination. A state is judged not by what it is but by what it does. And no state can rise above the moral values of its citizens. If we want a good state, good citizens must come first: this is where the section begins.

p071.s3.b1.q: no state can transcend the moral values of its citizenry as exemplified in their chosen leaders.

p071.s3.b2: The chosen people doctrine and national egotism have helped build nations, but no state can reach ideal levels until every form of intolerance is mastered. Intolerance is best combated by the co-ordination of science, commerce, play, and religion. The ideal state moves under three drives: love loyalty born of human brotherhood, intelligent patriotism based on wise ideals, and cosmic insight interpreted in terms of planetary facts.
p071.s3.b3: The laws of the ideal state are few, and instead of taboo they foster the positive liberty that comes from self-control. Leisure must produce as well as consume, and political service is esteemed as the highest devotion of the citizenry. The author sums it up: the best state governs least and co-ordinates most.

p071.s3.b4.q: That state is best which co-ordinates most while governing least.

p071.s3.b5: The ideals of statehood come by evolution, not revolution—by the slow growth of civic consciousness. At first people take up the burdens of government reluctantly, as a duty; later they seek such service as a privilege and the greatest honor. The author says the status of any civilization is faithfully portrayed by the caliber of the citizens who volunteer for the responsibilities of statehood.
p071.s4.h: IV. Progressive Civilization — Brotherhood and God-Consciousness
p071.s4.b0: On an evolutionary world, standing still means decay. The author lists the program of an expanding civilization: preserving individual liberty, protecting the home, economic security, preventing disease, compulsory education and employment, profitable use of leisure, care of the unfortunate, science and art, philosophy, and finally cosmic insight—spirituality. The list begins with material things and ends with spirit.

p071.s4.b1.q: Static conditions on an evolutionary world are indicative of decay;

p071.s4.b2: All this progress leads to two goals: socially, the brotherhood of man, and personally, God-consciousness, revealed in the supreme desire to do the will of the Father in heaven. Genuine brotherhood means a social order in which all delight in bearing one another’s burdens and truly desire to practice the golden rule.
p071.s4.b3: But the author warns against naive idealism. So long as some would exploit peaceful dispositions, the “golden rulers” must live by their ideals while keeping an adequate defense. The great test of idealism is to resist the temptation to use that military strength for aggression.

p071.s4.b4.q: Only love, brotherhood, can prevent the strong from oppressing the weak.

p071.s5.h: V–VI. The Evolution of Competition; The Profit Motive — Toward Co-operation and Service
p071.s5.b0: Competition is essential to social progress and is gradually displacing war, but unregulated it breeds violence. In early evolution competition stimulates, but in advanced civilizations co-operation is more efficient than competition. Even so, no attempt to eliminate the waste of competition should be allowed if it abrogates even the slightest of the individual’s basic liberties.
p071.s5.b1: The verdict on the profit motive has the same balance. An economy driven only by selfish profit is doomed unless profit motives are augmented by service motives, and it is incompatible with the teachings of Jesus. Yet the profit motive must not be suddenly removed before higher motives are firmly in place.

p071.s6.h: VII–VIII. Education; The Character of Statehood — From the Cradle to the Grave
p071.s6.b0: The enduring state is founded on culture, dominated by ideals, and motivated by service. Education must move from being localistic and success seeking to being world-wide and cosmic grasping, and it must be the business of a whole lifetime. The author sets out seven ascending levels of wisdom that education should lead toward, and says that through them many will rise to God-consciousness.
p071.s6.b1: In the ideal state philosophy will one day be the chief pursuit of its citizens. Control of education has passed from the clergy to lawyers and businessmen, but it must finally be given over to the philosophers and scientists, and teachers must be free beings and real leaders.

p071.s6.b2.q: The purpose of education should be acquirement of skill, pursuit of wisdom, realization of selfhood, and attainment of spiritual values.

p071.s6.b4: The final section names the only sacred feature of any human government: the division into executive, legislative, and judicial domains, the plan by which the universe itself is administered. On that basis the author lists twelve marks of progressive government, including the abolition of slavery, universal education, recognition of sex equality, a universal language, the ending of war through continental courts and a supreme planetary tribunal, and the evolution of a world religion presaging light and life.

p071.s6.b5.q: Urantia is far from the realization of these exalted ideals, but the civilized races have made a beginning—mankind is on the march toward higher evolutionary destinies.

p071.s7.b0: Paper 71 neither sanctifies nor despises the state. The state is an evolved tool, and its quality finally depends on the intelligence, morals, and spirit of service of its citizens. So the paper’s last message is addressed to people more than to politics. The ideal state draws nearer as we educate public opinion, keep learning all our lives, and enlarge profit into service, competition into co-operation, and patriotism into brotherhood.

p071.s7.b2: The series on human institutions that began in Paper 68 here gathers into a single vision: the long road on which bonds born of fear grow into brotherhood, and law born of taboo grows into the liberty of self-control. Paper 72 then makes the vision concrete by describing the government of a neighboring planet.

p072.s0.h: Introduction — Why Look at a Neighboring Planet?
p072.s0.b0: Paper 72 takes a form very rare in The Urantia Book. By permission of Lanaforge and with the approval of the Most Highs of Edentia, a Melchizedek describes the social, moral, and political life of the most advanced human race on a not far-distant planet of the Satania system. It is most unusual, the text says, for the system rulers to allow the affairs of one planet to be narrated on another.
p072.s0.b1: The permission was granted because of the likeness between the two worlds. That planet too was led astray in the Lucifer rebellion by the disloyalty of its Planetary Prince; it received a Material Son shortly after Adam came to Urantia, and he also defaulted; and since no Magisterial Son has ever been bestowed there, it remains isolated. So this paper is less a curious tale of a distant star than a case study of how far a world with similar wounds can advance on its own.

p072.s1.h: I. The Continental Nation — Five Hundred Years of Political Maturing
p072.s1.b0: The setting is an isolated continent about the size of Australia. Its population is about 140 million, a mixed race, predominantly blue and yellow, not yet fully blended but fraternizing well. The average length of life is ninety years, fifteen per cent higher than that of any other people on the planet. Heavy rains fall eight months of the year on high central mountains, favoring water power and irrigation, and the nation is self-sustaining, able to live indefinitely without imports.
p072.s1.b1: This nation was not ahead from the beginning. Thousands of years passed between the tribal stage and the rise of kings, and abortive republics, communal states, and dictators came and went endlessly. The turning point came about five hundred years ago, when one of three ruling dictators had a change of heart and volunteered to abdicate. A charter of liberty then grew up under a unified monarchy, the kings gradually became figureheads and finally disappeared, and the present republic has lasted two hundred years.

p072.s1.b2.q: This growth continued until about five hundred years ago when, during a politically fermenting period, one of the nation’s powerful dictator-triumvirs had a change of heart.

p072.s2.h: II. Political Organization — Divided Powers and a Three-House Legislature
p072.s2.b0: The central government is a strong federation of one hundred comparatively free states. State governors and legislators serve ten-year terms and cannot be re-elected, and no city may have more than one million inhabitants. The federal chief executive is elected every six years by universal suffrage and is advised by a supercabinet of all living ex-chief executives. Much administrative work is carried on by ten regional authorities, each an association of ten states.

p072.s2.b2: The judiciary is also twofold. Alongside the law courts—minor courts, state supreme courts, and the federal supreme court—stand the socioeconomic courts: parental courts, educational courts, and industrial courts. Having specialized tribunals for disputes in the home, the school, and the workplace reflects the idea that justice must reach every area of life, not only criminal law.
p072.s3.h: III–IV. The Home Life; The Educational System — The Basic Institution of Civilization
p072.s3.b0: These people regard the home as the basic institution of their civilization. It is against the law for two families to live under one roof, and attendance at parental schools of child culture is compulsory for both fathers and mothers. Fathers give almost as much attention to child culture as mothers do. All sex instruction is given at home, religious training is the exclusive privilege of parents, and there are no public places devoted exclusively to religious assembly.

p072.s3.b1.q: These people regard the home as the basic institution of their civilization.

p072.s3.b2.q: In their philosophy, religion is the striving to know God and to manifest love for one’s fellows through service for them,

p072.s3.b4: The schools have no classrooms. Only one study is pursued at a time, and after the first three years every pupil becomes an assistant teacher of those below. Books are consulted to solve problems that arise in the school shops and farms. Permission to marry is granted only a year after notice of intention and after both partners present certificates from the parental schools, and the divorce rate is only one tenth that of the civilized races of Urantia. Learning and preparation for family life are closely joined to the realities of living.

p072.s4.b0: The author frankly admits that the industrial situation is still far from these people’s ideals. Yet workers are increasingly becoming shareholders, violence has been outlawed as a means of settling disputes, and industrial courts pass on all conflicts. Slavery was abolished over a century ago by the gradual method of freeing two per cent each year. The most recent development is a principle for dividing earnings.

p072.s4.b2: People work six hours a day on a five-day week, four days of work and one of play. The profit motive is giving way to higher driving forces, and competition has shifted to play, skill, science, intellectual achievement, and social service. Even the richest man on the continent hurries after work to the school of statesmanship to qualify for public office. A new social disgust for idleness and unearned wealth is growing, and the people are learning to use their hard-won leisure for self-realization.

p072.s4.b3.q: Among this people public service is rapidly becoming the chief goal of ambition.

p072.s4.b4: There is also an effort to replace degrading charity with dignified old-age insurance. Pension funds come from one day’s earnings each month, bequests, the excess profits of compulsory labor in the mines, and half the income from natural resources. Betrayal of public trust is punished more heavily than any crime but treason and murder. In taxation, no property may be taxed more than one per cent of its value in a year, and the federal government cannot go into debt. How a government handles its people’s money reveals its morality.

p072.s4.b5.q: This nation is making a determined effort to replace the self-respect-destroying type of charity by dignified government-insurance guarantees of security in old age.

p072.s4.b6: The same spirit shows in matters of health and private life. In industry health receives first attention, but individual and family health remains a personal concern, and the government increasingly refrains from interfering in purely personal matters. Here we glimpse a sense of where public responsibility ends and personal freedom begins.
p072.s5.h: VIII–IX. The Special Colleges; The Plan of Universal Suffrage — A Democracy That Weighs Wisdom
p072.s5.b0: Every candidate for public office must be a graduate of a school of statesmanship. These schools are of three classes—national, regional, and state—and the offices a person may hold depend on the level of degree earned. Judges of the federal supreme court must hold degrees from all of them. There are also schools of philosophy, institutions of science, professional training schools, and military and naval schools.
p072.s5.b1: About fifty years ago these people saw a serious weakness in universal suffrage and modified their voting plan. Every citizen votes in two groups, one by economic function and one by social and philosophic inclination, and territorial voting was abandoned. Those who have rendered great service or shown extraordinary wisdom, and heavy taxpayers, receive additional votes, but no one may cast more than ten. Only the election of the chief executive is a nation-wide ballot of one vote each.

p072.s5.b2.q: The ideal state is organic, and every free and intelligent group of citizens represents a vital and functioning organ within the larger governmental organism.

p072.s6.h: X–XII. Dealing with Crime; Military Preparedness; The Other Nations — The Limits of Superiority
p072.s6.b0: Of this people’s methods of dealing with crime and defectives, the author himself says that some are pleasing but others will no doubt prove shocking to most Urantians. The text simply records severe measures—agricultural colonies, the death penalty, the prevention of reproduction among defectives—without offering them as a model for Urantia. In keeping with the text’s own attitude, this passage is best read as a reminder that even an advanced people’s institutions mix good and ill.
p072.s6.b1: In defense, restraint stands out. Military training is always paired with education in a trade or profession, so no professional military class can form. The nation keeps a powerful defense, yet for over a hundred years it has not used it in an offensive war; in the last two centuries it has fought only nine defensive conflicts. And it gives far more attention to training statesmen, scientists, and philosophers.

p072.s6.b2.q: They have become civilized to that point where they can vigorously defend civilization without yielding to the temptation to utilize their war powers in aggression.

p072.s6.b3: Yet on the other continents of this planet, eleven in all, the governments are decidedly inferior to the more advanced nations of Urantia. Now, for the first time, a great religious leader has arisen in this nation who advocates sending missionaries to its neighbors, and the author fears a repetition of the old mistake of forcing a superior culture and religion on others. Instead he suggests bringing the best of the neighboring peoples to be educated and then sending them home as emissaries of culture.

p072.s6.b4.q: We fear they are about to make the mistake that so many others have made when they have endeavored to force a superior culture and religion upon other races.

p072.s7.b0: This paper is not a blueprint for utopia. The author reminds us that the neighboring planet has had neither magisterial nor bestowal missions of the Paradise Sons, while Urantia, a bestowal world on which the Spirit of Truth has been poured out, is far better prepared to realize a planetary government and world-wide peace under law. The achievements of another world are not meant to discourage us but to make us aware of the greater spiritual resources we already have.

p072.s7.b1.q: and such an age is the planetary threshold to the utopian ages of light and life.

p072.s7.b3: With Paper 73 the story returns to Urantia and the preparation of the Garden of Eden. Remembering the struggles of this isolated world helps us appreciate more deeply what the mission of Adam and Eve was meant to bring to our own planet.
p073.lead: The garden on a Mediterranean peninsula that the workers of Van and Amadon prepared over eighty-odd years: the home awaiting Adam and Eve, the tree of life, and the Garden’s end.

p073.foot.text: Presented by Solonia, the seraphic “voice in the Garden”

p073.s0.h: Introduction — A Home Prepared Before They Came
p073.s0.b0: Paper 73 begins the story of Adam and Eve not with their arrival but with the home made ready to receive them. The Caligastia downfall brought cultural decadence and spiritual poverty, yet organic evolution went forward regardless. Almost forty thousand years ago the Life Carriers saw that the biologic progress of the Urantia races was nearing its apex, and together with the Melchizedek receivers they petitioned the Most Highs of Edentia to send a Material Son and Daughter.
p073.s0.b1: Tabamantia, sovereign supervisor of the series of experimental worlds, came to inspect the planet and duly recommended the request; in a little less than one hundred years Adam and Eve arrived. The paper is presented by Solonia, the seraphic “⟦Q 73:7.5⟧voice in the Garden.⟦/Q⟧” It shows how, on a world retarded by rebellion and resting under spiritual isolation, a small company of loyal people prepared the way for one who had not yet come.

p073.s1.h: I. The Nodites and the Amadonites — Two Surviving Streams of Culture
p073.s1.b0: On a normal planet the arrival of the Material Son heralds a great age of invention, material progress, and intellectual enlightenment—but not so on Urantia. Ten thousand years after the rebellion practically all the gains of the Prince’s administration had been effaced, and the tribes languished in savagery and moral stagnation. The traditions of Dalamatia and the culture of the Planetary Prince persisted among only two groups.

p073.s1.b2: After the destruction of Dalamatia the followers of Nod divided into three groups, settling near the headwaters of the Persian Gulf, in the highlands of Elam, and on the northeastern Syrian shores of the Mediterranean. They mated freely with the Sangik races and left an able progeny, and some of them, near Lake Van and the southern Caspian region, mingled with the Amadonites and were numbered among the “⟦Q 73:1.6⟧mighty men of old.⟦/Q⟧”
p073.s1.b3: A traditional enmity ran between the two groups, surfacing whenever they tried a common enterprise, and later in the affairs of Eden it was exceedingly difficult for them to work together in peace. Even so, before Adam and Eve came these were the most advanced peoples on earth. That even the keepers of culture could not be reconciled with one another shows that progress and harmony do not necessarily arrive together.

p073.s1.b4.q: Prior to the arrival of Adam and Eve these groups—Nodites and Amadonites—were the most advanced and cultured races on earth.

p073.s2.h: II. Planning for the Garden — A Preparation Begun in Faith
p073.s2.b0: Van knew that the Material Sons of Jerusem always lived in simple but charming garden homes. So, eighty-three years before the arrival of Adam and Eve, he proposed to his associates that they proclaim the advent and prepare a garden home for the newcomers. From the highland headquarters and sixty-one scattered settlements came more than three thousand workers, and Van divided them into one hundred companies, each with its captain.

p073.s2.b1.q: in solemn assembly, dedicated themselves to this mission of preparing for the promised—at least expected—Son.

p073.s2.b2: There was opposition. Caligastia and Daligastia, though deprived of much of their power for evil, did everything possible to frustrate the work. But the almost ten thousand loyal midway creatures labored tirelessly and largely offset their machinations. Beside the visible workers, unseen helpers were working too.
p073.s3.h: III. The Garden Site — A Mediterranean Peninsula, Almost an Island
p073.s3.b0: After nearly three years of searching, the committee on location reported on three possible sites: an island in the Persian Gulf, the river location later occupied as the second garden, and a long, narrow peninsula projecting westward from the eastern shores of the Mediterranean. The committee almost unanimously chose the third, and two years were spent moving the world’s cultural headquarters, including the tree of life, to the new site.
p073.s3.b1: Encircled by mountains and set like an island in an inland sea, the peninsula enjoyed a healthful climate and an even temperature. It seldom rained in Eden itself, but each night a mist rose from the irrigation channels to refresh the vegetation. The great river of the Garden flowed east, fed by four tributaries rising in the coastal hills—the “four heads” of the river that went out of Eden. The mountains held precious stones and metals, yet these received little attention; the dominant idea was to glorify horticulture and exalt agriculture.

p073.s3.b2.q: Eden was the one bright spot on Urantia

p073.s4.h: IV–V. Establishing the Garden; The Garden Home — A Garden, and Only a Garden
p073.s4.b0: Van gave the whole peninsula to the Garden and assigned pasturage and animal husbandry to the adjoining mainland. No animals were ever slaughtered within the Garden’s precincts. The first task was a brick wall across the neck of the peninsula; a smaller wall outside it enclosed wild beasts as an added defense. Every worker was a volunteer—no hirelings were ever used—and they supported themselves by cultivating the Garden and tending their herds.

p073.s4.b1.q: Van’s instructions were that Eden was to be a garden, and only a garden.

p073.s4.b2: The most human moment comes when Van suggests training the younger generation in case the expected Son and Daughter are delayed. To many this sounded like an admission of lack of faith; it caused great disappointment and many desertions. Yet Van went forward with his plan of preparedness, filling the vacant places with younger volunteers. True faith not only holds fast to its hope; it also has the faithfulness to prepare for that hope’s delay.

p073.s4.b4: When Adam came the Garden was only one-fourth finished, yet it had thousands of miles of irrigation ditches, more than twelve thousand miles of paved paths and roads, and just over five thousand brick buildings. Its sanitary arrangements were far ahead of anything yet attempted on Urantia, and Amadon’s inspectors made daily rounds in search of possible causes of sickness. Most of the Garden was deliberately left in a more or less natural state, since it was thought best to finish it according to Adam’s own ideas.
p073.s4.b5: By Adam’s arrival most of the plants of that part of the world were growing in Eden, and many fruits, cereals, and nuts had already been greatly improved. Many modern vegetables and cereals were first cultivated here. Adam and Eve were well pleased with the general plan of Eden, though they made many changes in the furnishings of their own dwelling.

p073.s4.b6.q: Never before this time nor after has Urantia harbored such a beautiful and replete exhibition of horticulture and agriculture.

p073.s5.h: VI. The Tree of Life — Not a Myth but a Gift of Edentia
p073.s5.b0: In the center of the Garden temple Van planted the long-guarded tree of life. The text draws a clear distinction: the “⟦Q 73:6.3⟧tree of the knowledge of good and evil⟦/Q⟧” may be a figure of speech, but the tree of life was real. It was a shrub of Edentia, sent to Urantia by the Melchizedeks when Caligastia was commissioned as Planetary Prince.

p073.s5.b1.q: The “tree of the knowledge of good and evil” may be a figure of speech, a symbolic designation covering a multitude of human experiences, but the “tree of life” was not a myth

p073.s5.b2: The tree stored space-energies antidotal to the age-producing elements of animal existence, but it was wholly useless to ordinary evolutionary beings. Its fruit served the materialized members of the Prince’s staff and the modified Andonites who possessed the complement of life, and Adam and Eve too ate of it periodically to maintain their dual form of physical life. So when the Nodites later invaded Eden and ate freely of the fruit for years with no effect, they became enraged, and in one of their internal wars the temple and the tree were both destroyed by fire.

p073.s5.b4.q: And now must all flesh on Urantia take the natural course of life and death.

p073.s5.b5: Adam, Eve, their children, and their children’s children all perished in the course of time and so came under the ascension scheme of the local universe, in which mansion world resurrection follows material death. The loss of the tree of life was not an ending; it meant that they entered the same path of ascension that every mortal walks.
p073.s6.h: VII. The Fate of Eden — A Garden Reclaimed by Nature
p073.s6.b0: After Adam left, the first garden was occupied in turn by Nodites, Cutites, and Suntites, and was overrun for almost four thousand years. Then, with the violent activity of the surrounding volcanoes and the submergence of the Sicilian land bridge to Africa, the eastern floor of the Mediterranean sank and carried the whole peninsula beneath the waters. The sinking was not sudden; it took several hundred years.

p073.s6.b1.q: We cannot regard this disappearance of the Garden as being in any way a result of the miscarriage of the divine plans or as a result of the mistakes of Adam and Eve.

p073.s6.b2: The Garden was never meant to be the permanent home of the Adamites. The Melchizedeks counseled Adam not to begin racial uplift until his family numbered half a million, and then to establish racial and continental headquarters under his sons and daughters. The Adamites were destined to go out as emissaries of new life, giving themselves unselfishly to the needy races of earth.

p073.s6.b3.q: They were to become emissaries of a new life to all the world

p073.s7.b0: The heroes of Paper 73 are not Adam and Eve but the people who waited for them. Van, Amadon, and thousands of volunteers worked for more than eighty years with no fixed date, and when some deserted they trained the next generation and carried on. The Garden they built was finally submerged, yet the text calls this a natural occurrence, not a failure. The worth of preparation lies not in its results lasting forever but in faithfully answering the call of one’s own time.

p073.s7.b2: Paper 74 turns to Adam and Eve, now arrived, and their first days in Eden. Remembering the labor of preparation seen in this paper helps us weigh more fully the expectations and misunderstandings they met, and the weight of the plan they had come to carry out.
p074.lead: The first six days and the 117-year reign of a Material Son and Daughter from Jerusem on an isolated world—and how the legend of a six-day creation arose.

p074.foot.text: Narrated by Solonia, the seraphic “voice in the Garden”

p074.s0.h: Introduction — Two Beings Made to Serve Together
p074.s0.b0: Paper 74 follows Adam and Eve from the moment of their arrival on Urantia through the life they built in Eden. They came 37,848 years before A.D. 1934, in midseason, when the Garden was at the height of bloom. The seraphic transports settled near the temple of the Father, and after ten days of rematerialization the two regained consciousness at the same moment. The narrator is the same seraphim as in the previous paper, Solonia.

p074.s0.b1.q: It is the essence of their service at all times and in all places never to be separated.

p074.s0.b2: This sentence is the key to the whole paper. Adam and Eve were designed to work as a pair, and most of the achievements and reforms the paper describes were accomplished by the two of them together. At the same time the paper ends by foreshadowing their default, so we read each scene with both hope and regret.
p074.s1.h: I. Adam and Eve on Jerusem — Volunteers Well Prepared
p074.s1.b0: The pair were members of the senior corps of Material Sons on Jerusem, jointly number 14,311, and a little more than eight feet tall. For more than fifteen thousand years they had directed the division of experimental energy as applied to the modification of living forms, and before that they had taught in the citizenship schools for new arrivals. The narrator asks us to bear this record in mind when we come to their later conduct.
p074.s1.b1: When volunteers were called for the Urantia mission, the entire senior corps volunteered, and the Melchizedek examiners made the final choice. Loyal to Michael during the Lucifer rebellion, Adam and Eve were nonetheless examined and thoroughly instructed before the System Sovereign, and were advised to regard themselves as subject to the Melchizedek receivers. They left behind one hundred children on Jerusem and departed amid the acclaim and well-wishing of its citizens.
p074.s2.h: II–III. Arrival of Adam and Eve; Adam and Eve Learn about the Planet — Welcome and Loneliness
p074.s2.b0: The first faces the pair saw on awakening were those of Van and Amadon. The tongue of Eden was an Andonic dialect that Van and Amadon had improved with a new alphabet of twenty-four letters, and Adam and Eve had mastered it before leaving Jerusem. Carrier pigeons spread the word that the promised Son had come; the senior Melchizedek delivered the charge of planetary custody; and Gabriel’s broadcast decreed the second judgment roll call as the third planetary epoch opened.
p074.s2.b1: Yet on the night of their welcome the two became painfully aware of their planetary isolation. The familiar broadcasts were silent, and every circuit of extraplanetary communication was absent. Their fellows had gone to well-ordered worlds, but here the fallen Planetary Prince was still present, shorn of most of his power yet still able to make their task difficult.

p074.s2.b2.q: they walked and talked far into the night, their first night on earth—and it was so lonely.

p074.s2.b4: The second day’s lesson is especially weighty. The two learned of the utter collapse of the Caligastia scheme for accelerating social evolution and came to see the folly of seeking progress apart from the divine plan. On the fourth day Eve shared with a man the honors and responsibilities of world affairs, which the text stresses was an astounding innovation, the first such thing on earth since the days of Dalamatia.

p074.s2.b5.q: They also arrived at a full realization of the folly of attempting to achieve planetary advancement independently of the divine plan of progression.

p074.s3.h: IV. The First Upheaval — Worship Belongs to the Father Alone
p074.s3.b0: The amazing events of those six days were too much even for the best minds of the world. On the night after the sixth day, the temporary administrators concluded that Adam and Eve were far too modest and unassuming—that they were in reality gods, or near enough to be worshiped. Van protested but was swept aside, and he sent the leader of the midwayers in haste to Adam. The people meant well; they simply could not understand the simplicity of their new rulers’ fraternal and democratic manner.

p074.s3.b1.q: Adam made it plain that he would accept any honor and receive all respect, but worship never!

p074.s3.b2: Just before noon on the seventh day, Adam and Eve pointed the people to the Father’s temple and bade them worship him who made us all. The pair stood alone on the mount with bowed heads while the people bowed down around the temple. This was the origin of the Sabbath-day tradition. The scene sets in sharp contrast the human tendency to make idols of leaders and the true leader’s way of turning that glory toward God.

p074.s4.h: V. Adam’s Administration — Between Ideal and Reality
p074.s4.b0: After almost seven years the Melchizedek receivers returned to Jerusem. Adam asked them several times to stay, but always the petitions were denied; the time had come for the Material Sons to assume full responsibility. Van and Amadon were translated that same night. Adam fostered the arts of manufacture to develop trade, and when Eden was disrupted over one hundred primitive manufacturing plants were in operation.
p074.s4.b1: But his efforts to establish a world government met stubborn resistance at every turn. Caligastia and Daligastia, deposed but not removed from the planet, opposed his work outside the Garden with well-planned resistance, and even within Eden some minds confused by the teaching of unbridled personal liberty upset his best plans. Adam had come to institute representative government but found none worthy of the name, and he fell back on Van’s method of organization.

p074.s4.b2.q: The sending of ambassadors from one tribe to another dates from the times of Adam.

p074.s5.h: VI–VII. Home Life of Adam and Eve; Life in the Garden — Play and the Golden Rule
p074.s5.b0: Before the default Eve bore sixty-three children, and when they left the Garden the family numbered four generations, 1,647 pure-line descendants. There was no cooking in Adam’s household; they ate fruits, nuts, and cereals once a day. Their bodies gave forth a shimmer of light, but since clothing obscured it only the glow from their heads could be seen—the origin of the halo tradition. They could exchange thoughts over about fifty miles, but this power was instantly suspended upon the mind’s surrender to the discord of evil.
p074.s5.b1: The sight of Adam’s children playing simply for the fun of it was something new on Urantia, and the text says that much of the play and humor of present-day races comes from the Adamic stock. The whole purpose of the western schools was socialization, while religious and sexual training were left to the home as the duty of parents.

p074.s5.b2.q: The play and humor of the present-day races are largely derived from the Adamic stock.

p074.s5.b3: The schools, and indeed every activity of the Garden, were always open to visitors. Unarmed observers could enter freely; to stay, a person had to be “adopted,” learning the plan of the Adamic bestowal and declaring loyalty to the social rule of Adam and the spiritual sovereignty of the Universal Father. It was a community that asked for both openness and commitment.

p074.s5.b5: The moral law differed little from the seven commandments of Dalamatia, but the Adamites taught deeper reasons for it; the indwelling of the Thought Adjuster, for instance, was given as an additional reason against taking human life. Adam taught personal prayer flowing from the soul rather than set prayers, and he tried to replace blood sacrifices with offerings of the fruit of the land, though with little progress.

p074.s5.b6.q: Adam did his best to discourage the use of set prayers, teaching that effective prayer must be wholly individual, that it must be the “desire of the soul”

p074.s5.b7.q: Adam definitely taught them that the woman, equally with the man, contributes those life factors which unite to form a new being.

p074.s5.b8: This was a great turning point for its time. Until then people assumed that all life came from the father and that the mother merely nurtured. Adam showed sex equality by the very way Eve worked at his side. The text soberly notes that Adam taught all his contemporaries could grasp, which was not very much, yet adds that even the small amount of imported blood brought tremendous gains.
p074.s6.h: VIII. The Legend of Creation — Adam’s Six Days Become Creation’s Six Days
p074.s6.b0: The last section traces the origin of the six-day creation story. It grew from the tradition that Adam and Eve spent just six days surveying the Garden—days not planned in advance but worked out one at a time. The choice of the seventh day for worship was wholly incidental to those events. The story of Eve made from Adam’s rib is a confused condensation of Adam’s arrival with the celestial surgery that accompanied the coming of the Prince’s staff.

p074.s6.b2: The text says that the idea of evolution is not a modern discovery. Away from the influence of Dalamatia and Eden, belief in gradual ascent was common, and many primitive tribes chose animals they took for ancestors as totems. The Old Testament account of creation dates from long after Moses and was shaped after the Babylonian captivity by a modified Mesopotamian version. The outlook of a golden age and a fall, the text judges, was discouraging because it rested on belief in retrogression rather than progression.

p074.s6.b3.q: The “golden age” is a myth, but Eden was a fact, and the Garden civilization was actually overthrown.

p074.s7.b0: Adam and Eve carried on in the Garden for one hundred and seventeen years. This paper carefully records what they achieved: an administration shared by men and women, the resolve to direct worship to God, schools that taught play and the golden rule. Then, in its final sentence, it foretells how the impatience of Eve and the errors of judgment of Adam led them to turn aside from the ordained way. Even a great beginning can falter when patience is lost—this is the lesson carried into the next paper.
